newsitem.title: DUBAI: Mideast Gulf Oil Outlook-Gas oil needs Indian summer.
newsitem.headline: Mideast Gulf Oil Outlook-Gas oil needs Indian summer.

text.p: The middle of the Gulf oil product barrel continues to suffer from a seasonal slump though renewed tendering by India for supplies starting August could provide much-needed support, Gulf-based oil traders said on Thursday.

Gas oil (diesel) talked at around $20 a barrel fob Gulf on Thursday, close to its lowest level since November 1995 and the spread to jet collapsing to a $1.50 discount. Diesel's spot premium was assessed between 20 cents and flat.
Diesel traded as high as $32 at the start of the year but has been dragged back by weaker crude markets and faltering demand in the key Singapore market.
The Gulf market was well supplied, compounded by spot sales from state-owned refiners and alternative supplies from the Mediterranean, traders said.

Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) had issued a tender to sell 75,000 tonnes of 0.5-percent sulphur gas oil and 30,000 tonnes of jet for late July liftings, Asian and Gulf-based traders said on Thursday.
Sellers pinned their hopes on Indian subcontinent demand.
India Oil Corp has issued a tender to buy up to 1.08 million tonnes of diesel for delivery between August 1997 and March 1998 in addition to its regular monthly spot import tender.
"India is appearing again as a strong market force. It could create some shorts in the market," one trader said.
Bangladesh Petroleum Corp's award of a tender to Kuwait Petroleum Corp (KPC) for the July-December supply of 3.3 million barrels of gas oil was also seen as supportive by Gulf traders.
"That should remove part of the Kuwaiti (spot) supply," said one trader in the Gulf.

Naphtha supplies from the region were sought after by Asian petrochemical firms, traders said. Gulf producers held out for higher term naphtha premiums after KPC drew a premium of $18 to Middle East quotes from August-July lifters, up from $7.90.
ADNOC had revised its offer to South Korean and Japanese naphtha customers a premium of $21 over its formula versus bids of around $19-20, traders said.
Far East traders on Thursday said that negotiations with ADNOC were deadlocked though some Gulf-based traders expected a deal to be clinched within the coming week.
ADNOC officials declined to comment on the talks.
Saudi Aramco had been able to carve a premium of around $15 for its Jubail-quality naphtha though it was struggling to place outstanding volumes, traders said.
Naphtha's spot Gulf market premium was steady at $10 though outright prices lost ground on weaker crude with talks around $180 a tonne fob Gulf on Thursday.
Fuel oil markets also remained steady with Fujairah 380-cst bunker market holding up at $95-97 a tonne on the back on good local tanker demand.
Saudi Aramco increased its A-960 bunker price from Ras Tanura and Dammam by $2 a tonne to $104 and National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC) raised its 280-cst Kharg price by $1 to $101.
